# One sample, a whole population {.divider background-color="#008CB7"}

[Act I · The tension]{.act}

::: {.notes}
This is the chapter on which every later chapter rests. Every regression table in the book reports a standard error, a t statistic, a p-value and a confidence interval, and all four are introduced here for the simplest possible estimator: the sample mean. If students master the logic for one mean, the regression chapters only change the estimator, not the reasoning.
:::

## We measure a sample, but we care about the population

We surveyed **171** women aged 30 who work full time and found mean earnings of **\$41,413**. We do not care about these 171 people as such. We care about *all* 30-year-old women working full time in the U.S. in 2010.

. . .

The sample mean $\bar{x}$ is our best guess of the population mean $\mu$, but it is only one draw: another sample of 171 would give a different number. **Statistical inference** turns that single number into a statement with quantified uncertainty, either a **range** (a confidence interval) or a **verdict on a claim** (a hypothesis test).

[The whole chapter answers one question: how far from $\mu$ could $\bar{x}$ plausibly be?]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Inference is the bridge from the sample we have to the population we want to describe. Stress that the population mean is a fixed, unknown number; what is random is the sample, and therefore the sample mean and every interval built from it.
:::

## One formula carries the whole chapter

$$t \;=\; \frac{\text{estimate} \;-\; \text{hypothesized value}}{\text{standard error}} \qquad\qquad \text{CI} \;=\; \text{estimate} \;\pm\; \text{critical value} \times \text{standard error}$$

::: {.incremental}
- The **estimate** here is $\bar{x}$ (or $\hat{p}$ for a proportion); in Chapter 7 it becomes a regression slope $b_2$
- The **standard error** measures how much the estimate would vary across repeated samples
- The **critical value** comes from the $t$ distribution (or the normal for proportions)
:::

[Learn this pair of formulas once and you can read every inference table in the book.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Key Takeaway 9 of the chapter: the methods generalize to other parameters. Point forward explicitly: in Chapter 7 the same t = (b − β*)/se(b) and b ± t × se(b) appear in every regression output.
:::

## Seven ideas anchor this chapter

::: {.incremental}
- **$H_0$ vs $H_a$**: the default claim we test, and the alternative we accept if it falls
- **Test statistic $t$**: how many standard errors the estimate sits from the value in $H_0$
- **$p$-value**: the probability of data at least this extreme *if $H_0$ were true*
- **Significance level $\alpha$**: the false-alarm rate we accept, usually $0.05$
- **Critical value**: the cutoff on $t$ that bounds the rejection region
- **Type I / Type II error**: a false alarm vs a missed effect; **power** $= 1-\beta$
- **Confidence interval**: the range of $\mu$ values a two-sided test would not reject
:::

[A test never *proves* $H_0$. It only asks whether the data can reject it.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
These are the chapter's Key Concepts glossary. Spend time on the p-value definition: it is a probability about the data computed under H0, never the probability that H0 is true.
:::

## A thread through every slide: three questions for any test

| Question | Answered by | Fails when… |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Is it real?** | $t$, $p$-value, CI | the gap is small relative to the SE |
| **Does it matter?** | the size of the gap, in units people care about | a precise estimate of a trivial gap |
| **Could we even tell?** | power, the width of the CI | a real gap hidden by a large SE |

[Every example in this deck gets all three questions. Statistical significance answers only the first.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
This is the recurring thread of the deck. Gas prices (4.5) are real and matter; female earnings vs $40,000 (4.4) might matter but we could not tell; Bolivia's mean IMDS vs 50 (CS2) is real but barely matters. The synthesis slide at the end puts every test on one ruler.
:::

# Section 4.1 · How precise is one sample mean? {#s41 .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Sample mean · standard deviation · standard error]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Section 4.1: the motivating example. Tools: the sample mean, the sample standard deviation, and the standard error.
:::

## The question: what do 30-year-old women earn? {.smaller}

**Data.** `AED_EARNINGS.DTA`: 171 women aged 30 working full time in the U.S. in 2010, annual earnings in dollars.

| Symbol | Name | Measures |
|:--|:--|:--|
| $\bar{x}$ | sample mean | our point estimate of the population mean $\mu$ |
| $s$ | sample standard deviation | how much **individual** earnings vary |
| $\text{se}(\bar{x}) = s/\sqrt{n}$ | standard error | how much the **sample mean** would vary across samples |

[Two different spreads: $s$ describes people; the standard error describes our estimate.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The data are a sample from a much larger population. The chapter's Key Concept 4.1: the standard error measures the precision of x̄ as an estimate of μ. Students regularly confuse s and se; this table is worth pausing on.
:::

## Earnings are right-skewed: a few high earners pull the mean up

![Earnings of the 171 women. The mean (\$41,413) sits above the median (\$36,000).](figures/fig_earn_hist.png)

[64% of the women earn less than the mean. Inference here is about the **mean**, which is not the typical earner.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Figure computed for these slides from the chapter's data. Earnings run from $1,050 to $172,000; skewness 1.71. With n = 171 the central limit theorem makes the sampling distribution of the mean close to normal even though earnings are skewed, so t-based inference is still reasonable. With very small samples from a skewed population it would not be.
:::

## Code: load the data and compute the standard error

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-3|4-6|7-10|11-14"}
import numpy as np                          # square roots
import pandas as pd                         # tabular data
from scipy import stats                     # t and normal distributions (used later)
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_EARNINGS.DTA"
data_earnings = pd.read_stata(url)          # 171 women aged 30, full-time, 2010
earnings = data_earnings["earnings"]        # annual earnings in dollars
n = len(earnings)                           # sample size
mean_earnings = earnings.mean()             # sample mean x-bar
std_earnings = earnings.std(ddof=1)         # sample std dev s (divides by n - 1)
se_earnings = std_earnings / np.sqrt(n)     # standard error = s / sqrt(n)
print(f"n = {n}")                           # 171
print(f"Mean: ${mean_earnings:,.2f}")       # point estimate of mu
print(f"Std dev: ${std_earnings:,.2f}")     # spread across women
print(f"Std error: ${se_earnings:,.2f}")    # spread of x-bar across samples
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
Self-contained: paste into an empty Colab cell. ddof=1 gives the sample standard deviation, dividing by n − 1 rather than n. Everything in sections 4.2–4.4 and 4.6 reuses these four numbers.
:::

## Output: a precise estimate from a noisy sample {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
| Statistic | Value |
|:--|--:|
| $n$ | 171 |
| Mean $\bar{x}$ | \$41,412.69 |
| Median | \$36,000.00 |
| Std. deviation $s$ | \$25,527.05 |
| Std. error $s/\sqrt{n}$ | [\$1,952.10]{.key} |

[$\text{se} = 25{,}527.05/\sqrt{171} = 1{,}952.10$]{.comment}
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
**How the SE scales with $n$** (same $s$):

| Sample size | SE |
|:--|--:|
| $n = 43$ (¼ as many) | \$3,893 |
| $n = 171$ (ours) | \$1,952 |
| $n = 684$ (4× as many) | \$976 |
:::
::::

[Individual earnings vary by about \$25,500, but the *average* of 171 of them varies by only about \$1,950.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The SE is 13 times smaller than s because √171 ≈ 13.1. With 43 women the SE would roughly double, to $3,893: not exactly 2 × 1,952 = 3,904, because 43 is slightly more than 171/4. In general, quartering the sample doubles the SE and quadrupling it halves the SE.
:::

## Reading the standard error

::: {.incremental}
- **Repeated-sampling meaning**: if we drew many samples of 171 women, their means would typically differ from $\mu$ by about \$1,950
- **Precision relative to the mean**: \$1,952 is under 5% of \$41,413, so the estimate is reasonably precise
- **Square-root law**: precision grows with $\sqrt{n}$, so halving the SE costs **four times** the data
:::

[Key Concept 4.1: the standard error is the single number behind every interval and test that follows.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The square-root law is why surveys get expensive: going from ±$3,900 to ±$1,950 needs 4× the sample, and to ±$975 needs 16×.
:::

## What the standard error assumes

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### It requires
- a **random sample**: each woman is an independent draw from the population
- the formula $s/\sqrt{n}$ is built on **independence**
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### It does not capture
- **non-sampling error**: misreported earnings, non-response
- **dependence**: clustered or time-series data need other SEs (Ch. 7, 12, 17)
:::
::::

[The SE measures sampling noise only, and only under independence. GDP growth in 4.5 will show what happens when independence fails.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Standard caveat. The formula is derived for independent draws. Survey data with clusters, or time series where this quarter resembles the last, violate it, and the s/√n formula then understates the real uncertainty.
:::

# Section 4.2 · Why a $t$ ruler, not a normal one? {#s42 .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[$t$ statistic · degrees of freedom · fat tails]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Section 4.2: the t statistic and the t distribution. Tools: standardizing the sample mean, degrees of freedom, critical values.
:::

## The $t$ statistic standardizes the sample mean

$$t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{\text{se}(\bar{x})} = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{s/\sqrt{n}} \;\sim\; T(n-1)$$

::: {.incremental}
- If we knew $\sigma$, $(\bar{x}-\mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt{n})$ would be standard normal
- We **estimate** $\sigma$ by $s$, and that extra uncertainty fattens the tails: the $t$ distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom
- Exact when the population is normal; otherwise a good approximation for moderate $n$ (central limit theorem)
:::

[Fatter tails mean bigger critical values: the price of not knowing $\sigma$.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Key Concept 4.2. The degrees of freedom are n − 1 because one degree of freedom is used to estimate the mean before computing s.
:::

## The $t$ distribution approaches the normal as $n$ grows

![Panel A: $t(4)$ has much fatter tails than the standard normal. Panel B: $t(30)$ is already close to it.](figures/fig_4-2_01.png)

[With 4 degrees of freedom, values beyond ±2 are over twice as likely as under the normal.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Chapter Figure 4.1. Numbers computed for these slides: P(|T| > 2) is 11.6% for t(4), 5.5% for t(30) and 4.6% for the standard normal.
:::

## Code: critical values for different degrees of freedom

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|2-4|5-6"}
from scipy import stats                     # t and normal distributions
for df in [4, 9, 30, 99, 170]:              # degrees of freedom = n - 1
    t_crit = stats.t.ppf(0.975, df)         # 97.5th percentile: two-sided 5% cutoff
    print(f"df = {df:>3}: t critical = {t_crit:.3f}")
z_crit = stats.norm.ppf(0.975)              # the normal's cutoff, for comparison
print(f"normal:   z critical = {z_crit:.3f}")   # 1.960
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

[Computed for these slides; Exercise 3 of the chapter asks for the $n = 10$ and $n = 100$ cases.]{.comment}

::: {.notes}
Self-contained. ppf is the inverse CDF (percent-point function): it returns the cutoff with a given probability below it. 0.975 leaves 2.5% in the upper tail, which is the two-sided 5% critical value.
:::

## Output: by $n = 171$ the $t$ cutoff is almost the normal's

| Degrees of freedom | Sample size $n$ | 5% two-sided critical value |
|:--|--:|--:|
| 4 | 5 | 2.776 |
| 9 | 10 | 2.262 |
| 30 | 31 | 2.042 |
| 99 | 100 | 1.984 |
| 170 | 171 | [1.974]{.key} |
| normal ($\infty$) | — | 1.960 |

[For our sample the $t$ critical value 1.974 is within 1% of 1.96, which is why the "estimate ± 2 SE" rule of thumb works.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The rule of thumb in the chapter: for n > 30, t(n−1, 0.025) ≈ 2. The correction matters only for small samples: with 10 observations the cutoff is 2.26, so using 1.96 would give intervals that are too narrow.
:::

# Section 4.3 · What values of $\mu$ are plausible? {#s43 .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Confidence intervals · margin of error · the confidence–precision trade-off]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Section 4.3: confidence intervals. Tools: the CI formula, the correct repeated-sampling interpretation, and the trade-off between confidence and width.
:::

## A confidence interval is estimate ± margin of error

$$\bar{x} \;\pm\; t_{n-1,\,\alpha/2} \times \text{se}(\bar{x})$$

::: {.incremental}
- $t_{n-1,\,\alpha/2}$: the critical value; for 95% confidence, $\alpha = 0.05$ and we leave 2.5% in each tail
- **Margin of error** $= t_{n-1,\,\alpha/2} \times \text{se}(\bar{x})$
- **Meaning**: if we repeated the sampling many times, about 95% of the intervals built this way would contain $\mu$
:::

[The interval is random; $\mu$ is fixed. The 95% describes the *method*, not this one interval.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Key Concept 4.3. The phrase "we are 95% confident" is shorthand for the repeated-sampling property. Rule of thumb for n > 30: x̄ ± 2 × se.
:::

## Code: the 95% confidence interval for mean earnings

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-5|6-8|9-11|12-13"}
import numpy as np                          # square roots
import pandas as pd                         # tabular data
from scipy import stats                     # t distribution
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_EARNINGS.DTA"
earnings = pd.read_stata(url)["earnings"]   # 171 women, annual earnings
n = len(earnings)                           # sample size
mean_earnings = earnings.mean()             # x-bar
se_earnings = earnings.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n)    # s / sqrt(n)
conf_level = 0.95                           # confidence level
alpha = 1 - conf_level                      # 0.05
t_crit = stats.t.ppf(1 - alpha/2, n - 1)    # critical value t(170, 0.025)
margin_of_error = t_crit * se_earnings      # half-width of the interval
print(mean_earnings - margin_of_error, mean_earnings + margin_of_error)  # the CI
```

::: {.notes}
Self-contained. The chapter's code is identical except that it reuses the variables from section 4.1.
:::

## Output: \$37,559 to \$45,266 {.smaller}

| Component | Value |
|:--|--:|
| Sample mean $\bar{x}$ | \$41,412.69 |
| Standard error | \$1,952.10 |
| Critical value $t_{170,\,0.025}$ | 1.9740 |
| Margin of error $1.9740 \times 1{,}952.10$ | \$3,853.48 |
| **95% confidence interval** | [[\$37,559.21,&nbsp;\$45,266.17]]{.key} |

[Width \$7,707 · computed with the $t(170)$ distribution]{.comment}

[The data are consistent with any population mean between about \$37,600 and \$45,300.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The interval excludes $36,000 and $46,000, so those values are implausible for μ, while $40,000 lies comfortably inside. That last fact will reappear as the result of the hypothesis test in section 4.4.
:::

## Reading the interval right

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Correct
- 95% of intervals built this way, across repeated samples, contain $\mu$
- "We are 95% confident $\mu$ is between \$37,559 and \$45,266", as shorthand for the above
- The interval reflects **sampling** uncertainty only
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Wrong
- "There is a 95% probability that $\mu$ is in **this** interval"
- "95% of women earn between \$37,559 and \$45,266"
- "The interval contains 95% of the data"
:::
::::

[The interval is about the **mean**. Individual earnings range from \$1,050 to \$172,000.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The second wrong reading is the most common in student work. Contrast the CI width (~$7,700) with the standard deviation of individual earnings (~$25,500).
:::

## Simulation: 39 of 40 intervals catch the mean

![Each line is the 95% CI from one simulated sample of 171, resampled from the 171 earnings as if they were the population. The pink interval misses.](figures/fig_ci_coverage.png)

[Each interval either contains $\mu$ or it does not. The 95% is the long-run hit rate of the procedure.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Simulation made for these slides (seed 42), in the spirit of Exercise 8 of the chapter. We treat the 171 observed earnings as the population (so its mean $41,413 is the "true" μ) and draw 40 samples of 171 with replacement. With 40 intervals we expect about 2 misses; we got 1. Even though earnings are skewed, the t interval works well at n = 171.
:::

## Code: the same data at 90%, 95% and 99% confidence

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|2-4|5-8|9"}
# continues from the previous block (n, mean_earnings, se_earnings defined)
for conf in [0.90, 0.95, 0.99]:              # three confidence levels
    alpha = 1 - conf                        # tail probability, split in two
    t_crit = stats.t.ppf(1 - alpha/2, n - 1)    # larger for higher confidence
    ci_lower = mean_earnings - t_crit * se_earnings   # lower bound
    ci_upper = mean_earnings + t_crit * se_earnings   # upper bound
    width = ci_upper - ci_lower             # full width of the interval
    label = f"{conf*100:.0f}%"              # "90%", "95%", "99%"
    print(f"{label:<5} t={t_crit:.3f} [{ci_lower:,.2f}, {ci_upper:,.2f}] width {width:,.2f}")
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
Only the critical value changes between the three lines; the estimate and its standard error are the same.
:::

| 90% | 1.654 | \$38,184.17 | \$44,641.21 | \$6,457.03 |
| 95% | 1.974 | \$37,559.21 | \$45,266.17 | \$7,706.97 |

[Going from 90% to 99% confidence makes the interval 58% wider. Only a larger sample buys both confidence and precision.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Width ratio 10,170.68 / 6,457.03 = 1.575. With n = 684 (4× larger) every interval would be about half as wide. 95% is the convention in economics; 99% is used when a false claim would be costly, 90% for exploratory work.
:::

# Section 4.4 · Is $\mu = \$40{,}000$ credible? {#s44 .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Two-sided test · $p$-value · critical value · Type I and II errors · power]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Section 4.4: the two-sided hypothesis test. Tools: H0 and Ha, the test statistic, the two equivalent decision rules, the duality with the confidence interval, the two kinds of error, and power.
:::

## A hypothesis test asks whether a claim survives the data

$$H_0: \mu = \mu_0 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: \mu \neq \mu_0 \qquad\qquad t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\text{se}(\bar{x})} \sim T(n-1) \text{ if } H_0 \text{ is true}$$

::: {.incremental}
- **$p$-value rule**: $p = 2 \times \Pr[T_{n-1} \geq |t|]$; reject $H_0$ if $p < \alpha$
- **Critical-value rule**: reject $H_0$ if $|t| > t_{n-1,\,\alpha/2}$
- The two rules **always agree**, and both agree with the CI: reject exactly when $\mu_0$ lies outside the $100(1-\alpha)\%$ interval
:::

[The test measures the gap between estimate and claim in **standard errors**, then asks how unusual that gap would be if the claim were true.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Key Concept 4.4. The example: H0: μ = $40,000 against Ha: μ ≠ $40,000 at α = 0.05.
:::

## Code: test $H_0: \mu = \$40{,}000$

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-6|7|8|9|10|11-13"}
import numpy as np                          # square roots
import pandas as pd                         # tabular data
from scipy import stats                     # t distribution
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_EARNINGS.DTA"
earnings = pd.read_stata(url)["earnings"]   # 171 women, annual earnings
n, mean_earnings = len(earnings), earnings.mean()          # n and x-bar
se_earnings = earnings.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n)            # standard error
mu0 = 40000                                 # hypothesized value under H0
t_stat = (mean_earnings - mu0) / se_earnings               # distance in SEs
p_value = 2 * (1 - stats.t.cdf(abs(t_stat), n - 1))        # two-sided p-value
t_crit_95 = stats.t.ppf(0.975, n - 1)       # critical value for alpha = 0.05
print(f"t = {t_stat:.4f}, p = {p_value:.4f}, critical = ±{t_crit_95:.4f}")
print("Reject H0" if p_value < 0.05 else "Do not reject H0")   # the decision
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
Self-contained. stats.t.cdf(|t|, n − 1) is the probability below |t|; one minus it is the upper-tail area, doubled for a two-sided test.
:::

## Output: we do not reject $H_0$ {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
| | Value |
|:--|--:|
| $\bar{x} - \mu_0$ | \$1,412.69 |
| Standard error | \$1,952.10 |
| $t$-statistic | [0.7237]{.key} |
| $p$-value (two-sided) | 0.4703 |
| Critical value | ±1.9740 |
| Decision at $\alpha = 0.05$ | do not reject |

[$\$40{,}000$ lies inside the 95% CI [\$37,559, \$45,266]]{.comment}
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
![](figures/fig_x_01.png)
:::
::::

[The sample mean is less than one standard error from \$40,000, an ordinary amount of sampling noise.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Both rules agree: p = 0.4703 > 0.05, and |t| = 0.72 < 1.974. If μ really were $40,000, a sample mean at least this far from it (in either direction) would occur about 47% of the time.
:::

## What "do not reject" does and does not mean

::: {.incremental}
- **It means**: the data are *consistent* with $\mu = \$40{,}000$
- **It does not mean** $\mu = \$40{,}000$: \$41,000, \$43,000 or \$45,000 are consistent too; the CI lists them all
- **The $p$-value is not** $\Pr[H_0 \text{ true}]$: it is the probability of a gap at least this large *if* $H_0$ were true
- The result could be a **Type II error**: a real difference that this sample is too small to detect
:::

[Key Concept 4.6: "fail to reject" is not "accept". Report the confidence interval, which says how large a difference the data still allow.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. The interval allows a population mean as much as $5,266 above $40,000.
:::

## Two ways to be wrong {.smaller}

| | $H_0$ true in reality | $H_0$ false in reality |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Reject $H_0$** | **Type I error** (false alarm), probability $\alpha$ | correct: **power** $= 1-\beta$ |
| **Do not reject $H_0$** | correct, probability $1-\alpha$ | **Type II error** (missed effect), probability $\beta$ |

::: {.incremental}
- We **choose** $\alpha$ (e.g. 0.05); $\beta$ depends on $n$, on the true gap, and on $\alpha$
- Lowering $\alpha$ to 0.01 cuts false alarms but **raises** $\beta$; raising it to 0.10 does the reverse
- Only a **larger sample** (or a larger true effect) lowers both at once
:::

[In the earnings test we did not reject, so the only mistake we could have made is a Type II error.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Choose α by the cost of each error. Medical trials, where a false claim is very costly, use α = 0.01; exploratory work sometimes uses 0.10. The usual target for power is 80% (β = 0.20).
:::

## Code: how likely was this test to detect a real gap?

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|2-3|4-7|8"}
# continues from the previous block (earnings, mu0 defined) — computed for these slides
s = earnings.std(ddof=1)                    # sample std dev, treated as known
for n_size in [171, 684]:                   # our sample, and 4x larger
    se = s / np.sqrt(n_size)                # standard error at this n
    df, c = n_size - 1, stats.t.ppf(0.975, n_size - 1)   # df and 5% critical value
    nc = (41412.69 - mu0) / se              # gap in SEs if the true mean were $41,412.69
    power = stats.nct.sf(c, df, nc) + stats.nct.cdf(-c, df, nc)   # P(|T| > c)
    print(f"n = {n_size}: power = {power:.3f}")   # probability of rejecting H0
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
Power is not computed in the chapter, which discusses it in words; this calculation is added for the slides. If the true mean were $41,412.69, the test statistic would follow a noncentral t distribution with noncentrality (μ − μ0)/se. Power is the probability that |T| exceeds the critical value. stats.nct is scipy's noncentral t.
:::

|:--|--:|--:|
| \$41,413 | [0.11]{.key} | 0.30 |
| \$45,000 | 0.72 | 1.00 |

[Power of the two-sided 5% test of $\mu = \$40{,}000$]{.comment}

**Smallest gap detected with 80% power:**

- \$5,500 with $n = 171$
- \$2,738 with $n = 684$
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](figures/fig_power.png)
:::
::::

[Even if \$41,413 were the truth, the test would reject only 11% of the time. Failing to reject here says more about the sample size than about $\mu$.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Computed for these slides. The chapter's own reasoning (Key Concepts glossary): quadrupling the sample would double t to about 1.45, still below 1.96. The power curve makes that precise: with 684 women the power at μ = $41,413 is still only 0.30. At n = 684, μ = $45,000 the power is 0.9992, shown as 1.00. Power equals α = 0.05 exactly at μ = μ0.
:::

# Section 4.5 · Three tests on real questions {#s45 .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Gas prices · male earnings · GDP growth]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Section 4.5 applies the same two-sided test to three new datasets, and gives three very different answers. Each is a chance to ask the thread's three questions: is it real, does it matter, could we tell?
:::

## Same test, three datasets, three different lessons {.smaller}

| Example | Data | $H_0$ | $t$ | $p$ | Decision | Lesson |
|:--|:--|:--|--:|--:|:--|:--|
| Gas prices | 32 stations, Yolo County | $\mu = \$3.81$ | [−5.26]{.key} | <&nbsp;0.0001 | reject | a small gap can be very precise |
| Male earnings | 191 men aged 30 | $\mu = \$50{,}000$ | 0.50 | 0.617 | do not reject | heavy tails, imprecise mean |
| GDP growth | 241 quarters, U.S. | $\mu = 2.0\%$ | −0.07 | 0.946 | do not reject | dependent data, SE too small |

[One recipe, three verdicts. The interpretation always depends on the data behind the numbers.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Key Concept 4.7: the testing pattern is the same across applications; meaning comes from context. The next slides take each example through its own arc.
:::

## Gas prices: are Yolo County prices different from the state's?

**Question.** Is the mean price at Yolo County gas stations different from the California average of \$3.81 per gallon?

**Data.** `AED_GASPRICE.DTA`: 32 stations in three cities (West Sacramento 15, Davis 10, Woodland 7).

$$H_0: \mu = 3.81 \qquad H_a: \mu \neq 3.81 \qquad t \text{ with } 31 \text{ degrees of freedom}$$

[A two-sided question: prices could be higher or lower than the state average.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter frames this as the classic statistical-vs-practical significance example. The critical value with 31 degrees of freedom is 2.04, a little above 1.96 because the sample is small.
:::

## Code: test the gas-price claim

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-5|6-9|10-12|13"}
import numpy as np                          # square roots
import pandas as pd                         # tabular data
from scipy import stats                     # t distribution
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_GASPRICE.DTA"
price = pd.read_stata(url)["price"]         # price per gallon at 32 stations
mean_price = price.mean()                   # sample mean
std_price = price.std(ddof=1)               # sample std dev
n_price = len(price)                        # 32 stations
se_price = std_price / np.sqrt(n_price)     # standard error
mu0_price = 3.81                            # California state average
t_stat_price = (mean_price - mu0_price) / se_price               # distance in SEs
p_value_price = 2 * (1 - stats.t.cdf(abs(t_stat_price), n_price - 1))   # two-sided p
print(f"mean {mean_price:.4f}, se {se_price:.4f}, t {t_stat_price:.4f}, p {p_value_price:.6f}")
```

::: {.notes}
Self-contained; the chapter's code.
:::

## Output: a 14-cent gap, more than five standard errors wide {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
| | Value |
|:--|--:|
| $n$ | 32 |
| Mean | \$3.6697 |
| Std. dev. | \$0.1510 |
| Std. error | \$0.0267 |
| $t$ | [−5.2577]{.key} |
| $p$ (two-sided) | 0.00001 |
| 95% CI | [\$3.615,&nbsp;\$3.724] |
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](figures/fig_gas.png)
:::
::::

[Reject $H_0$: Yolo County prices are lower than the state average, and \$3.81 lies far outside the 95% CI.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
p = 0.0000103, which the chapter prints as 0.0000 and describes as < 0.0001. The 95% CI (computed for these slides, with t(31) = 2.04) runs from $3.615 to $3.724. The figure shows every station; the white band is the CI for the mean, not for individual prices.
:::

## Is it real, and does it matter?

::: {.incremental}
- **Real?** Yes: $t = -5.26$. Prices barely vary across stations (SD 15¢), so the SE is under 3¢ and a 14-cent gap is easy to detect
- **Does it matter?** 14¢ × 15 gallons = **\$2.10 per tank**; with 52 fill-ups a year, about **\$109 a year**: meaningful for a household
- **Could we tell?** Yes, easily: high power from a small SE, even with only 32 stations
:::

[Key Concept 4.5: a small difference can be highly significant when it is precisely measured. Significance is about the gap relative to its SE, not its size.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter's practical-significance arithmetic uses the rounded 14¢ gap: 0.14 × 15 = $2.10; × 52 = $109.20. With the unrounded gap of 14.03¢ the yearly figure is $109.44.
:::

## Caveats on the gas-price test

::: {.incremental}
- **Sampling**: 32 stations in three cities, not a random sample of all county stations; West Sacramento alone is almost half the sample
- **Timing**: one snapshot; the state average must refer to the same period for the comparison to be fair
- **The benchmark is itself an estimate**: \$3.81 is treated as a known constant
- The test says Yolo prices are lower **on average**; one station sells at \$4.09
:::

[A $p$-value of 0.00001 settles the sampling-noise question only. It cannot fix a non-random sample or a mismatched benchmark.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Standard caveats. The city counts come from the data's city variable. If prices were collected on one day and the state average refers to a monthly mean, part of the gap could reflect timing rather than location.
:::

## Male earnings: do 30-year-old men earn more than \$50,000?

**Data.** `AED_EARNINGSMALE.DTA`: 191 men aged 30 working full time, 2010.

**The chapter's test** is two-sided:

$$H_0: \mu = 50{,}000 \qquad H_a: \mu \neq 50{,}000$$

[The question is **directional** ("more than"), so its natural form is one-sided; the chapter defers that to section 4.6. These slides report both.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter computes the two-sided test here and notes that a one-sided test is more appropriate. Section 4.6 then runs its one-sided example on the female earnings data instead, so the one-sided p-value for men is computed for these slides.
:::

## Code: test the male-earnings claim

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-5|6-9|10-13|14-15"}
import numpy as np                          # square roots
import pandas as pd                         # tabular data
from scipy import stats                     # t distribution
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_EARNINGSMALE.DTA"
earnings_male = pd.read_stata(url)["earnings"]   # 191 men, annual earnings
mean_male = earnings_male.mean()            # sample mean
std_male = earnings_male.std(ddof=1)        # sample std dev
n_male = len(earnings_male)                 # 191
se_male = std_male / np.sqrt(n_male)        # standard error
mu0_male = 50000                            # hypothesized value
t_stat_male = (mean_male - mu0_male) / se_male                      # distance in SEs
p_value_male = 2 * (1 - stats.t.cdf(abs(t_stat_male), n_male - 1)) # two-sided p
p_upper_male = 1 - stats.t.cdf(t_stat_male, n_male - 1)             # one-sided (Ha: mu > 50,000)
print(f"mean {mean_male:,.2f}, se {se_male:,.2f}, t {t_stat_male:.4f}")   # estimate and t
print(f"two-sided p {p_value_male:.4f}, one-sided p {p_upper_male:.4f}")   # both p-values
```

:::

## Why the male-earnings test has so little power

::: {.incremental}
- **Heavy tails**: three men are recorded at \$498,000, the data's top code, and one at \$1; the SD (\$65,035) is 2.5× the women's
- The mean (\$52,354) sits far above the median (\$38,000); without the three top-coded men it would be \$45,243
- A large SD means a large SE, so a gap of \$2,354 is only half a standard error
:::

[Not rejecting here is mostly a statement about noise. A mean driven by three people is a fragile target for inference.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter lists three possible reasons for not rejecting: H0 true, insufficient power, high variability. The data point strongly to the third. The mean excluding the three top-coded observations is a simple descriptive check computed for these slides, not a recommended estimator; with top coding the true mean is, if anything, higher than the sample mean. Medians and other robust summaries come later in the book.
:::

## GDP growth: has U.S. growth averaged 2% a year?

**Data.** `AED_REALGDPPC.DTA`: U.S. real GDP per capita, **quarterly**, 1959Q1–2020Q1. The variable `growth` is the **year-over-year** growth rate, so it starts in 1960Q1: **241 quarterly observations**.

$$H_0: \mu = 2.0 \qquad H_a: \mu \neq 2.0 \quad (\text{percent per year})$$

[Note what the 241 observations are: overlapping four-quarter growth rates, not 241 separate years.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Verified from the data: growth equals 100 × (realgdppc_t / realgdppc_(t−4) − 1). Each observation shares three of its four quarters with the previous one, so consecutive observations are strongly correlated. So the 241 observations are not 241 independent years; the data cover about 60 years.
:::

## Code: test the 2% benchmark

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-5|6-9|10-12|13-14"}
import numpy as np                          # square roots
import pandas as pd                         # tabular data
from scipy import stats                     # t distribution
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_REALGDPPC.DTA"
growth = pd.read_stata(url)["growth"].dropna()   # first 4 quarters have no YoY growth
mean_growth = growth.mean()                 # average growth, % per year
std_growth = growth.std(ddof=1)             # sample std dev
n_growth = len(growth)                      # 241 quarters
se_growth = std_growth / np.sqrt(n_growth)  # SE, assuming independent observations
mu0_growth = 2.0                            # benchmark under H0
t_stat_growth = (mean_growth - mu0_growth) / se_growth                    # distance in SEs
p_value_growth = 2 * (1 - stats.t.cdf(abs(t_stat_growth), n_growth - 1))  # two-sided p
print(f"mean {mean_growth:.4f}, se {se_growth:.4f}, t {t_stat_growth:.4f}, p {p_value_growth:.4f}")
print(f"lag-1 autocorrelation {growth.autocorr(1):.2f}")   # neighbouring quarters move together
```

## Output: the mean is 1.99%, but the observations are not independent {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
| | Value |
|:--|--:|
| $n$ (quarters) | 241 |
| Mean | 1.9905% |
| Std. dev. | 2.1781 |
| Std. error (i.i.d.) | 0.1403 |
| $t$ | [−0.0680]{.key} |
| $p$ (two-sided) | 0.9458 |
| 95% CI (i.i.d.) | [1.71%,&nbsp;2.27%] |
| Lag-1 autocorrelation | 0.87 |
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](figures/fig_gdp_ts.png)
:::
::::

[Do not reject 2%. But with a lag-1 correlation of 0.87, the i.i.d. standard error understates the true uncertainty.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The CI and the autocorrelation are computed for these slides. The figure shows long swings (recessions in 1974–75, 1980–82, 2008–09), not independent draws around a mean. A rough rule of thumb for an AR(1) series gives an "effective" sample of n(1 − ρ)/(1 + ρ) ≈ 17 independent observations rather than 241; the right standard error (HAC, Chapters 12 and 17) would be several times larger than 0.14.
:::

## Not rejecting does not "validate" the 2% benchmark

::: {.incremental}
- **Real?** No evidence of a difference from 2%, so the result is "consistent with 2%", not "2% confirmed"
- **Could we tell?** Less than the output suggests: the SE of 0.14 assumes 241 independent observations, but neighbouring quarters overlap
- **Does it matter?** Yes: 1.5% versus 2.5% growth compounds into very different living standards over 60 years
:::

[Key Concept 4.6 applies here too: the data fail to reject 2%, but that does not show the long-run rate *is* 2%. With dependent data, report a wider interval.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Failing to reject never confirms H0, and the 241 overlapping observations carry far less information than 241 independent draws. The chapter makes both points (non-rejection is not proof; with a lag-1 autocorrelation of about 0.87 the i.i.d. t-test is only approximate) and points to Chapter 17; these slides put that caveat up front.
:::

# Section 4.6 · Does $\mu$ *exceed* \$40,000? {#s46 .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[One-sided (directional) tests · upper and lower tails]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Section 4.6: one-sided tests. Tools: upper- and lower-tailed hypotheses, one-tail p-values and critical values, and when a one-sided test is legitimate.
:::

## A directional claim puts the whole rejection region in one tail {.smaller}

| Test | $H_0$ | $H_a$ | $p$-value | Reject if |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Upper-tailed | $\mu \leq \mu^*$ | $\mu > \mu^*$ | $\Pr[T_{n-1} \geq t]$ | $t > t_{n-1,\,\alpha}$ |
| Lower-tailed | $\mu \geq \mu^*$ | $\mu < \mu^*$ | $\Pr[T_{n-1} \leq t]$ | $t < -t_{n-1,\,\alpha}$ |
| Two-sided | $\mu = \mu^*$ | $\mu \neq \mu^*$ | $2\Pr[T_{n-1} \geq \lvert t \rvert]$ | $\lvert t \rvert > t_{n-1,\,\alpha/2}$ |

::: {.incremental}
- The claim we want to establish goes in $H_a$
- All of $\alpha$ sits in one tail, so the critical value is smaller: **1.654** instead of **1.974** for $n = 171$
- If $t$ has the sign $H_a$ predicts, the one-sided $p$ is **half** the two-sided $p$; if not, it is **above 0.5**
:::

[One-sided tests are more powerful in the chosen direction and blind in the other.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Key Concept 4.8. The "half the two-sided p-value" rule holds only when the estimate falls on the side Ha predicts. Case Study 1, Task 4 shows the opposite case.
:::

## Code: upper-tailed test of $H_a: \mu > \$40{,}000$

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-6|7|8|9|10|11"}
import numpy as np                          # square roots
import pandas as pd                         # tabular data
from scipy import stats                     # t distribution
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_EARNINGS.DTA"
earnings = pd.read_stata(url)["earnings"]   # 171 women, annual earnings
n, se_earnings = len(earnings), earnings.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(earnings))   # n and SE
mu0 = 40000                                 # H0: mu <= 40,000
t_stat = (earnings.mean() - mu0) / se_earnings     # same t as the two-sided test
p_value_upper = 1 - stats.t.cdf(t_stat, n - 1)     # upper-tail area only
t_crit_upper = stats.t.ppf(0.95, n - 1)     # all 5% in the upper tail
print(f"t = {t_stat:.4f}, one-sided p = {p_value_upper:.4f}, critical = {t_crit_upper:.4f}")
```

Self-contained. Note 0.95 instead of 0.975 in the critical value: no splitting of α between two tails.

|:--|--:|--:|
| $t$-statistic | 0.7237 | 0.7237 |
| $p$-value | [0.2351]{.key} | 0.4703 |
| Critical value | 1.6539 | ±1.9740 |
| Decision | do not reject | do not reject |

[$0.2351 = 0.4703 / 2$, because $t > 0$ points the way $H_a$ predicts]{.comment}
:::

![](figures/fig_x_02.png)
:::
::::

[We cannot conclude that mean earnings exceed \$40,000. The gap is small relative to its SE, whichever test we use.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The figure is the chapter's one-sided visualization: the shaded upper tail holds all 5%, cut off at 1.654. The observed t = 0.72 is well short of it.
:::

## When is a one-sided test legitimate?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Use it when
- theory or policy fixes the direction **before** seeing the data
- only one direction would change a decision (a drug *better* than placebo; a policy that *raises* income)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Avoid it when
- either direction would be interesting
- the field reports two-sided tests (economics usually does)
- you switch **after** seeing a two-sided $p = 0.08$ to get a one-sided $p = 0.04$: that is $p$-hacking
:::
::::

[Decide the direction before looking at the data. A one-sided test chosen afterwards has a true false-alarm rate of 10%, not 5%.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
If a researcher picks the tail after seeing which way the estimate points, they effectively run a two-sided test at the 10% level while reporting 5%. That is why the choice must be pre-specified.
:::

# Section 4.7 · Is the race tied? {#s47 .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Proportions · binary data · the $z$ test]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Section 4.7: proportions. Tools: the sample proportion as a mean of 0/1 data, its standard error, the normal-based CI and z test.
:::

## A proportion is just the mean of 0/1 data

$$\hat{p} = \bar{x} = \frac{\#\text{yes}}{n} \qquad \text{se}(\hat{p}) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}} \qquad \text{CI: } \hat{p} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\,\text{se}(\hat{p})$$

::: {.incremental}
- Code each voter 1 (Democrat) or 0 (not): $\hat{p}$ is the sample mean and the variance is $\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})$
- With large $n$ (rule of thumb: $n\hat{p} \geq 10$ and $n(1-\hat{p}) \geq 10$) use the **normal** critical value, 1.96
- To test $H_0: p = p_0$, use the SE **implied by $H_0$**: $z = (\hat{p} - p_0)/\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}$
:::

[Everything learned about means carries over; only the SE formula changes.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Key Concept 4.9. Two different SEs appear: the CI uses p̂(1 − p̂)/n, the test uses p0(1 − p0)/n because under H0 we know the variance. With p̂ = 0.521 and p0 = 0.5 they are almost identical (0.01646 vs 0.01648).
:::

## Code: 480 of 921 voters intend to vote Democrat

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-2|3-6|7-9|10-16"}
import numpy as np                          # square roots
from scipy import stats                     # normal distribution
n_total = 921                               # voters polled
n_success = 480                             # intend to vote Democrat
p_hat = n_success / n_total                 # sample proportion
se_prop = np.sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n_total)   # SE at p-hat (for the CI)
z_crit = 1.96                               # normal critical value, 95%
ci_lower_prop = p_hat - z_crit * se_prop    # lower bound
ci_upper_prop = p_hat + z_crit * se_prop    # upper bound
p0 = 0.50                                   # H0: tied race
se_under_h0 = np.sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / n_total)     # SE implied by H0
z_stat = (p_hat - p0) / se_under_h0         # z statistic
p_value_prop = 2 * (1 - stats.norm.cdf(abs(z_stat)))   # two-sided p (normal)
print(f"p_hat {p_hat:.4f}, se {se_prop:.4f}")   # estimate and its SE
print(f"95% CI [{ci_lower_prop:.4f}, {ci_upper_prop:.4f}]")   # interval
print(f"z {z_stat:.4f}, p {p_value_prop:.4f}")   # test of a tied race
```

## Output: 52.1%, but a tie cannot be ruled out {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
| | Value |
|:--|--:|
| $\hat{p}$ | 0.5212 |
| SE | 0.0165 |
| 95% CI | [0.4889,&nbsp;0.5534] |
| Margin of error | ±3.2 pp |
| $z$ (vs 0.50) | 1.2851 |
| $p$-value | [0.1988]{.key} |

[$n\hat{p} = 480$, $n(1-\hat{p}) = 441$: both far above 10]{.comment}
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](figures/fig_prop.png)
:::
::::

[Do not reject a tied race: the CI [48.9%, 55.3%] contains 50%. The lead is 2.1 percentage points with a ±3.2-point margin.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
z = 1.29: the sample proportion is 1.29 standard errors above 50%. About a 20% chance of a gap at least this large if the race were truly tied. The lower bar in the figure is the chapter's what-if, discussed on the next slide.
:::

## Same share, bigger poll: when does 52% become significant?

::: {.incremental}
- The chapter's what-if: the **same** share, 52%, from **2,500** voters
- SE falls to 0.010; 95% CI [50.0%, 54.0%]; $z = 2.00$, $p = 0.045$: **significant at 5%, only just**
- With the exact $\hat{p} = 0.5212$ instead of 0.52: $z = 2.12$, $p = 0.034$
:::

[Nothing about the voters changed, only the sample size. Statistical significance is as much about $n$ as about the effect.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter's numbers use p̂ rounded to 0.52; the exact-p̂ version is computed for these slides. Either way the lower CI bound sits a hair above 50% (50.04% with p̂ = 0.52), so "significant" here is a knife-edge call. Practical side: a 2-point lead matters a great deal in an election, so this is a case where the effect may matter even when we cannot yet tell.
:::

## Caveats on polls

::: {.incremental}
- The SE covers **sampling error** only; non-response and people who change their minds are not in it
- "Intend to vote" is not "will vote": the population of voters differs from the population polled
- The normal approximation needs $n\hat{p}$ and $n(1-\hat{p})$ both large; for rare events use exact methods
:::

[The reported margin of error (±3.2 points) is a floor on the real uncertainty, not a ceiling.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Standard caveats for proportions from surveys. The same logic applies to employment rates, approval ratings or market shares.
:::

# Case Study 1 · Has world labor productivity changed? {#cs1 .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Mendez convergence-clubs data · 108 countries · 1990 and 2014 · six tasks]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Case Study 1 applies every tool of the chapter to cross-country productivity. The chapter gives the tasks as fill-in templates and outlines without output; every task is run here, with the blanks filled in, and its output reported. Results not printed in the chapter are therefore all "computed for these slides".
:::

## The question: productivity growth and gaps across countries {.smaller}

**Data.** Mendez (2020) convergence-clubs panel: **108 countries × 25 years (1990–2014) = 2,700 observations**. We use labor productivity `lp` (output per worker, in dollars) for 1990 and 2014, and `region`.

| Task | Question | Tool (section) |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | Range of mean productivity in 2014? | CI, 95% vs 99% (4.3) |
| 2 | Did mean productivity change, 1990 → 2014? | two-sample and paired $t$ tests (4.4) |
| 3 | Is Africa below Europe? | two-sample test, CI for a difference |
| 4 | Does the 2014 mean exceed \$50,000? | one-sided test (4.6) |
| 5 | Did more than half of countries grow? | proportions (4.7) |
| 6 | Which regions differ? | many tests, multiple testing |

[Six tasks, one dataset: the chapter's whole toolkit on a development question.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Economic context: the convergence hypothesis says poorer countries should grow faster than richer ones. The tasks test levels and changes of mean productivity; they do not test convergence directly, which needs growth-on-initial-level regressions (later chapters).
:::

## Code: load the panel and extract the two cross-sections

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-4|5-7|8-9|10-12"}
import numpy as np                          # square roots
import pandas as pd                         # tabular data
from scipy import stats                     # t and normal distributions
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt             # plots
url = ("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/"            # Mendez (2020) repository
       "mendez2020-convergence-clubs-code-data/master/assets/dat.csv")
df = pd.read_csv(url).set_index(["country", "year"])     # panel indexed by country-year
lp_1990 = df.loc[df.index.get_level_values("year") == 1990, "lp"]   # productivity, 1990
lp_2014 = df.loc[df.index.get_level_values("year") == 2014, "lp"]   # productivity, 2014
print(f"Observations: {len(df):,}; countries: {df.index.get_level_values('country').nunique()}")
print(f"1990: n={len(lp_1990)}, mean={lp_1990.mean():,.0f}, std={lp_1990.std():,.0f}")
print(f"2014: n={len(lp_2014)}, mean={lp_2014.mean():,.0f}, std={lp_2014.std():,.0f}")
```

## Task 1 code: 95% and 99% CIs for 2014 (template filled)

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|2-5|6-8|9-11|12-14"}
# continues from the previous block
n_2014 = len(lp_2014)                       # 108 countries
mean_2014 = lp_2014.mean()                  # blank 1: sample mean
std_2014 = lp_2014.std()                    # blank 2: sample std dev
se_2014 = std_2014 / np.sqrt(n_2014)        # standard error
t_crit_95 = stats.t.ppf(1 - 0.05/2, df=n_2014 - 1)   # blank 3: df = n - 1
me_95 = t_crit_95 * se_2014                 # 95% margin of error
ci_95 = (mean_2014 - me_95, mean_2014 + me_95)       # blanks 4-5: the bounds
t_crit_99 = stats.t.ppf(1 - 0.01/2, df=n_2014 - 1)   # 99% critical value
me_99 = t_crit_99 * se_2014                 # 99% margin of error: wider
ci_99 = (mean_2014 - me_99, mean_2014 + me_99)       # 99% bounds
se_1990 = lp_1990.std() / np.sqrt(len(lp_1990))      # 1990 for comparison
me_1990 = stats.t.ppf(0.975, df=len(lp_1990) - 1) * se_1990   # 1990 margin
print(ci_95, ci_99, 2 * me_95, 2 * me_1990)          # bounds and widths
```

| | Mean | 95% CI | 95% width | 99% CI | 99% width |
|:--|--:|:--|--:|:--|--:|
| 2014 | \$40,977 | [[\$34,519,&nbsp;\$47,435]]{.key} | \$12,915 | [\$32,434,&nbsp;\$49,520] | \$17,086 |
| 1990 | \$23,224 | [\$19,392,&nbsp;\$27,056] | \$7,664 | [\$18,154,&nbsp;\$28,293] | \$10,139 |

[$t_{107,\,0.025} = 1.982$, $t_{107,\,0.005} = 2.623$; $n = 108$ in both years · computed for these slides]{.comment}

::: {.incremental}
- The 99% CI is **wider** (the template's last blank): more confidence costs width
- The 2014 interval is **69% wider** than 1990's because countries became more dispersed, with the same $n$
- The two 95% intervals do not overlap: a first hint that the mean changed
:::

[Precision depends on dispersion as well as sample size: same 108 countries, much less precise mean.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Width ratio 12,915/7,664 = 1.685, equal to the ratio of standard deviations (33,853/20,089) because n is the same. Non-overlapping intervals imply a significant difference, but overlapping ones would not imply the opposite; Task 2 runs the proper test.
:::

## Task 2 code: did mean productivity change? Two tests

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|2-4|5-7|8-9|10-13"}
# continues from the previous block
se_1990, se_2014 = lp_1990.std() / np.sqrt(108), lp_2014.std() / np.sqrt(108)   # each SE
se_diff = np.sqrt(se_1990**2 + se_2014**2)  # blanks 1-2: SE of the difference
t_stat = (lp_2014.mean() - lp_1990.mean()) / se_diff   # blanks 3-4: Welch t
t_scipy, p_scipy = stats.ttest_ind(lp_2014, lp_1990, equal_var=False)   # blanks 5-6
print(f"Welch: diff {lp_2014.mean() - lp_1990.mean():,.0f}, se {se_diff:,.0f}")
print(f"       t {t_scipy:.3f}, p {p_scipy:.2e}")              # blank 7: Reject
# computed for these slides: the same 108 countries appear in both years
x14, x90 = lp_2014.droplevel("year"), lp_1990.droplevel("year")   # align by country
t_pair, p_pair = stats.ttest_rel(x14, x90)  # paired test = one-sample t on the changes
change = x14 - x90                          # within-country change
print(f"Paired: mean change {change.mean():,.0f}, se {change.std() / np.sqrt(108):,.0f}")
print(f"        t {t_pair:.3f}, p {p_pair:.2e}")   # paired test result
```

The chapter's own discussion question notes that the 1990 and 2014 samples contain the same countries and suggests a paired test; the paired test is computed for these slides. droplevel("year") removes the year from the index so that the two Series line up by country.

## Task 2 output: same verdict, but the paired test is far sharper {.smaller}

| | Welch (independent samples) | Paired (same countries) |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Mean change, 1990 → 2014 | \$17,753 | \$17,753 |
| SE of the change | \$3,788 | [\$1,628]{.key} |
| $t$ | 4.687 | [10.904]{.key} |
| Degrees of freedom | 174.0 | 107 |
| $p$-value | 0.000006 | <&nbsp;10⁻¹⁸ |
| 95% CI for the change | [\$10,277,&nbsp;\$25,229] | [\$14,526,&nbsp;\$20,981] |

[Paired results computed for these slides · Welch is the chapter's template]{.comment}

[Reject $H_0$ either way: mean productivity rose by about \$17,800 (+76%). Pairing cuts the SE by 57%.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The Welch test treats the two years as independent samples, so its SE includes the huge differences between rich and poor countries. The paired test looks only at within-country changes. The point estimate is identical; only the standard error, and therefore t, p and the CI, differ.
:::

## Why pairing helps: each country is compared with itself

![Each dot is a country: 1990 productivity (x) against 2014 (y). Dots above the dashed 45° line grew.](figures/fig_cs1_paired.png){height="430"}

[The two years are correlated 0.93: rich countries stayed rich. Differencing removes that shared level, leaving only the change.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The SD of the within-country changes ($16,920) is smaller than either year's SD ($20,089 and $33,853) because the two years are so highly correlated. That is why the paired SE is less than half the Welch SE. Economically: the average country's output per worker rose by about $17,800. Correlation computed for these slides.
:::

## Task 3 code: Africa versus Europe in 2014

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|2-4|5|6-9|10-12"}
# continues from the previous block
df_2014 = df.loc[df.index.get_level_values("year") == 2014]       # 2014 cross-section
lp_africa = df_2014.loc[df_2014["region"] == "Africa", "lp"]      # 26 countries
lp_europe = df_2014.loc[df_2014["region"] == "Europe", "lp"]      # 30 countries
t_stat, p_val = stats.ttest_ind(lp_africa, lp_europe, equal_var=False)   # Welch test
v_a, v_e = lp_africa.var() / len(lp_africa), lp_europe.var() / len(lp_europe)   # s^2/n
diff = lp_africa.mean() - lp_europe.mean()  # difference in means
se_diff = np.sqrt(v_a + v_e)                # SE of the difference
df_w = (v_a + v_e)**2 / (v_a**2 / (len(lp_africa) - 1) + v_e**2 / (len(lp_europe) - 1))  # Welch df
t_c = stats.t.ppf(0.975, df_w)              # critical value at the Welch df
print(f"diff {diff:,.0f}, t {t_stat:.2f}, p {p_val:.1e}")              # gap and test
print(f"95% CI [{diff - t_c*se_diff:,.0f}, {diff + t_c*se_diff:,.0f}]")   # CI for the gap
```

## Task 4 code: does the 2014 mean exceed \$50,000?

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|2-3|4|5|6-7"}
# continues from the previous block
res_greater = stats.ttest_1samp(lp_2014, popmean=50000, alternative="greater")   # Ha: mu > 50,000
res_two = stats.ttest_1samp(lp_2014, popmean=50000, alternative="two-sided")     # Ha: mu != 50,000
res_less = stats.ttest_1samp(lp_2014, popmean=50000, alternative="less")         # for contrast only
print(f"mean {lp_2014.mean():,.0f}, t {res_greater.statistic:.3f}")              # t is negative
print(f"p (greater) {res_greater.pvalue:.4f}, p (two-sided) {res_two.pvalue:.4f}")  # chapter's
print(f"p (less) {res_less.pvalue:.4f}")    # never switch to this after seeing t
```

## Task 4 output: when the estimate points the wrong way {.smaller}

| $H_a$ | $t$ | $p$-value | Decision at 5% |
|:--|--:|--:|:--|
| $\mu > 50{,}000$ (the chapter's claim) | −2.770 | [0.9967]{.key} | do not reject |
| $\mu \neq 50{,}000$ | −2.770 | 0.0066 | reject |
| $\mu < 50{,}000$ (not pre-specified) | −2.770 | 0.0033 | — |

[Sample mean \$40,977 · one-sided critical value 1.659 · computed for these slides]{.comment}

::: {.incremental}
- The mean is **below** \$50,000, so $t < 0$ and the upper-tail $p$ is $1 - 0.0066/2 = 0.9967$, not half the two-sided $p$
- We **cannot** conclude productivity exceeds the benchmark; the two-sided test says it differs, on the low side
- Switching to $H_a: \mu < 50{,}000$ after seeing the sign would be $p$-hacking
:::

[A one-sided $p$-value above 0.5 means the data point *against* the direction you hoped for.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
This answers the chapter's discussion question: here the one-sided p-value is larger than the two-sided one because the estimate falls on the side opposite to Ha. Type I error in this context: if the true mean were at or below $50,000, a 5% test would wrongly declare it above the benchmark at most 5% of the time.
:::

## Task 5 code: what share of countries grew?

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|2-3|4-6|7-8|9-10"}
# continues from the previous block
growth = (lp_2014.droplevel("year") > lp_1990.droplevel("year")).astype(int)   # 1 if lp rose
n = len(growth)                             # 108 countries
p_hat = growth.mean()                       # share of growth winners
se_p = np.sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n)     # SE at p-hat (for the CI)
ci = (p_hat - 1.96 * se_p, p_hat + 1.96 * se_p)       # 95% normal CI
z = (p_hat - 0.5) / np.sqrt(0.5 * 0.5 / n)  # z test of H0: p = 0.5
p_val = 2 * stats.norm.sf(abs(z))           # two-sided p-value
print(f"{growth.sum()} of {n}: p_hat {p_hat:.3f}, CI [{ci[0]:.3f}, {ci[1]:.3f}]")   # share
print(f"z {z:.2f}, p {p_val:.1e}")          # test of H0: p = 0.5
```

## Task 6 code: every region, every pair

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-2|3-6|7-10|11-13"}
# continues from the previous block (df_2014 from Task 3)
import itertools                            # all pairs of regions
by_region = df_2014.groupby("region")["lp"]                         # 5 regions
stats_r = by_region.agg(["count", "mean", "std"])                   # n, mean, s
stats_r["se"] = stats_r["std"] / np.sqrt(stats_r["count"])          # SE of each mean
stats_r["tc"] = stats.t.ppf(0.975, stats_r["count"] - 1)            # t critical, df = n - 1
for a, b in itertools.combinations(sorted(stats_r.index), 2):        # 10 pairs
    xa = df_2014.loc[df_2014["region"] == a, "lp"]                  # region a
    xb = df_2014.loc[df_2014["region"] == b, "lp"]                  # region b
    print(a, b, stats.ttest_ind(xa, xb, equal_var=False))           # Welch test
stats_r["lo"] = stats_r["mean"] - stats_r["tc"] * stats_r["se"]    # lower 95% bound
stats_r["hi"] = stats_r["mean"] + stats_r["tc"] * stats_r["se"]    # upper 95% bound
print(stats_r.round(0))                     # the CI table
```

| Americas − Asia | −\$5,889 | −0.72 | 0.473 | | |
| Africa − Oceania | −\$63,856 | −5.68 | 0.095 | | |
| Americas − Oceania | −\$42,230 | −3.48 | 0.110 | | |
| Asia − Oceania | −\$36,341 | −2.87 | 0.119 | | |
| Europe − Oceania | −\$2,495 | −0.21 | 0.861 | | |

[Welch tests · computed for these slides]{.comment}

[With 10 tests at 5%, the chance of at least one false alarm is up to 40%. Here the same 5 pairs survive the Bonferroni cutoff of 0.005.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Family-wise error rate for 10 independent tests: 1 − 0.95^10 = 0.401. Bonferroni divides α by the number of tests: 0.05/10 = 0.005. Every pair involving Oceania is insignificant despite gaps of up to $64,000, because two observations give almost no information: a large, possibly important, difference that we simply cannot detect. That is the "could we tell?" question again.
:::

## Case Study 1: what the six tasks add up to

::: {.incremental}
- **Change over time**: mean productivity rose by about \$17,800 (+76%); the paired test makes this unmistakable ($t = 10.9$)
- **Regional gaps**: Europe is far ahead; Africa, the Americas and Asia are significantly behind it; Americas vs Asia cannot be told apart
- **Breadth**: 97 of 108 countries grew; all 11 that did not were in the poorer half in 1990
- **Method lessons**: pair when units repeat; one-sided tests can point the wrong way; many tests inflate false alarms; tiny groups give useless intervals
:::

[The right test depends on how the data were generated: same countries twice is not two independent samples.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
On convergence: these tasks show large and persistent level gaps, and that the countries that fell back all started in the poorer half. A proper convergence test (does initial productivity predict growth?) needs regression, from Chapter 5 onward.
:::

# Case Study 2 · Is Bolivia's development equal across departments? {#cs2 .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[DS4Bolivia · 333 municipalities · 9 departments · six tasks]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Case Study 2 brings the chapter's tools to subnational development in Bolivia. The chapter's code cells for Tasks 1–6 are run here and their outputs reported; Cohen's d and the Welch variant in Task 5 are computed for these slides.
:::

## The question: does municipal development differ across Bolivia's departments? {.smaller}

**Data.** DS4Bolivia (`ds4bolivia_v20250523.csv`): 339 municipalities; **333** have complete data on the five variables used. Outcome: the **Municipal Sustainable Development Index (IMDS)**, 0–100.

| Task | Question | Tool |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | National mean IMDS? | 95% CI |
| 2 | Is the average municipality at the midpoint, 50? | two-sided one-sample test |
| 3 | Which departments differ? | CI per department, forest plot |
| 4 | Is La Paz above the national mean? | one-sided test |
| 5 | How large is the gap between top and bottom departments? | two-sample test |
| 6 | What should a policy brief say? | summary table |

[Same toolkit, new question: statistical significance versus policy relevance.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter's text says the dataset covers 339 municipalities, which is correct for the file; the analysis sample after dropna() on mun, dep, imds, ln_NTLpc2017 and pop2017 has 333. Department sizes range from 11 (Tarija) to 87 (La Paz).
:::

## Code: load the data and summarize IMDS

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-4|5-6|7-8|9-10"}
import numpy as np                          # square roots
import pandas as pd                         # tabular data
from scipy import stats                     # t distribution
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt             # forest plot
url_bol = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/ds4bolivia/master/ds4bolivia_v20250523.csv"
bol = pd.read_csv(url_bol)                  # 339 municipalities, 350+ columns
key_vars = ["mun", "dep", "imds", "ln_NTLpc2017", "pop2017"]   # variables used here
bol_key = bol[key_vars].dropna().copy()     # complete cases: 333 municipalities
print(bol_key["imds"].describe().round(2))  # IMDS summary statistics
print(bol_key["dep"].value_counts().sort_index())   # municipalities per department
```

## Tasks 1–2 code: national CI and the midpoint test

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|2-4|5|6|7-8"}
# continues from the previous block
n = len(bol_key["imds"])                    # 333 municipalities
x_bar = bol_key["imds"].mean()              # national mean IMDS
se = bol_key["imds"].std() / np.sqrt(n)     # standard error
ci_low, ci_high = stats.t.interval(0.95, df=n - 1, loc=x_bar, scale=se)   # Task 1: 95% CI
t_stat, p_value = stats.ttest_1samp(bol_key["imds"], popmean=50)          # Task 2: H0: mu = 50
print(f"mean {x_bar:.4f}, se {se:.4f}, CI [{ci_low:.4f}, {ci_high:.4f}]")
print(f"t {t_stat:.4f}, p {p_value:.6f}")   # reject H0 if p < 0.05
```

::: {.notes}
The chapter's Task 1 and Task 2 cells combined. stats.t.interval builds x̄ ± t × se directly; ttest_1samp computes the same t statistic as section 4.4.
:::

## Tasks 1–2 output: significantly above 50, by about one point {.smaller}

| Task | Result |
|:--|:--|
| 1 · Mean IMDS | 51.1580 (SE 0.3704) |
| 1 · 95% CI | [50.43,&nbsp;51.89] |
| 2 · $H_0: \mu = 50$ | $t$ = [3.1258]{.key}, $p$ = 0.0019 → reject |
| 2 · Gap from 50 | 1.16 points on a 0–100 scale |

::: {.incremental}
- **Real?** Yes: 50 lies outside the 95% CI, $t = 3.13$
- **Does it matter?** Barely: the average municipality is 1.2 points above the midpoint
- **Could we tell?** Easily: 333 municipalities give an SE of 0.37, so even a one-point gap stands out
:::

[Key Concept 4.12 in action: a large sample makes a small, policy-irrelevant gap statistically significant.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter's interpretation: we are 95% confident that the true mean municipal development index lies between 50.43 and 51.89. Caveat: the 333 municipalities are essentially the whole population of Bolivian municipalities, not a random sample; the "population" here is a conceptual one (the process generating municipal outcomes). Also, 50 is a scale midpoint, not a policy target, so rejecting it has limited meaning.
:::

## Task 3 code: a CI for each department

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|2-3|4-5|6-7|8"}
# continues from the previous block
dept_stats = (bol_key.groupby("dep")["imds"]                  # one row per department
              .agg(["mean", "std", "count"]).sort_values("mean"))   # mean, s, n
dept_stats["se"] = dept_stats["std"] / np.sqrt(dept_stats["count"])          # SE per department
dept_stats["t_crit"] = stats.t.ppf(0.975, df=dept_stats["count"] - 1)        # df = n - 1 each
dept_stats["ci_low"] = dept_stats["mean"] - dept_stats["t_crit"] * dept_stats["se"]    # lower
dept_stats["ci_high"] = dept_stats["mean"] + dept_stats["t_crit"] * dept_stats["se"]   # upper
print(dept_stats[["mean", "se", "ci_low", "ci_high", "count"]].round(2))     # the table
```

## Task 4 code: is La Paz above the national mean?

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|2-3|4|5|6"}
# continues from the previous block
la_paz = bol_key[bol_key["dep"] == "La Paz"]["imds"]   # 87 municipalities
national_mean = bol_key["imds"].mean()      # 51.16, treated as a fixed benchmark
t_stat_lp, p_two = stats.ttest_1samp(la_paz, popmean=national_mean)   # two-sided first
p_one = p_two / 2 if t_stat_lp > 0 else 1 - p_two / 2   # one-sided, Ha: mu_LP > national
print(f"La Paz mean {la_paz.mean():.4f}, t {t_stat_lp:.4f}, one-sided p {p_one:.4f}")
```

| | Value |
|:--|--:|
| La Paz municipalities | 87 |
| La Paz mean IMDS | 50.98 |
| National mean (benchmark) | 51.16 |
| $t$ | −0.312 |
| One-sided $p$ ($H_a$: above) | [0.622]{.key} |

::: {.incremental}
- La Paz's mean is slightly **below** the national mean, so the one-sided $p$ exceeds 0.5: no evidence La Paz is more developed
- **Caveat**: the benchmark includes La Paz itself (87 of 333 municipalities, 26%) and is treated as a known constant; a two-sample comparison of La Paz versus the rest would be cleaner
:::

[Housing the seat of government does not make the department's *municipalities* more developed on average.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Most of La Paz's 87 municipalities are rural; the cities of La Paz and El Alto count as just two of them. A department mean weights every municipality equally, regardless of population, so it describes the typical municipality, not the typical person.
:::

## Task 5 code: the top department versus the bottom one

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|2-4|5-6|7|8-13"}
# continues from the previous block
dept_means = bol_key.groupby("dep")["imds"].mean()   # mean IMDS by department
top_dept, bot_dept = dept_means.idxmax(), dept_means.idxmin()   # Tarija and Pando
top_values = bol_key[bol_key["dep"] == top_dept]["imds"]         # 11 municipalities
bot_values = bol_key[bol_key["dep"] == bot_dept]["imds"]         # 13 municipalities
t_stat_2s, p_value_2s = stats.ttest_ind(top_values, bot_values)  # pooled-variance test (chapter)
t_w, p_w = stats.ttest_ind(top_values, bot_values, equal_var=False)   # Welch, for comparison
n1, n2 = len(top_values), len(bot_values)   # group sizes
pooled_var = ((n1 - 1) * top_values.var() + (n2 - 1) * bot_values.var()) / (n1 + n2 - 2)
sp = np.sqrt(pooled_var)                    # pooled standard deviation
gap = top_values.mean() - bot_values.mean() # the development gap
print(f"gap {gap:.2f}, t {t_stat_2s:.3f}, p {p_value_2s:.1e}")   # chapter's test
print(f"Welch t {t_w:.3f}, p {p_w:.1e}, Cohen's d {gap / sp:.2f}")   # added checks
```

## Task 6: what the policy brief should say

::: {.incremental}
- **Differences are real**: Tarija (60.6) and Santa Cruz (54.3) lead; Pando (45.9), Potosí (47.6) and Chuquisaca (47.8) lag, with CIs excluding the national mean of 51.2
- **Some are not policy-relevant**: the national mean is significantly above 50, but by only 1.2 points
- **Precision is uneven**: Tarija and Pando rest on 11 and 13 municipalities; their CIs are about 7 points wide
- **Limits**: municipalities are not people (no population weights); the 333 are nearly the whole country; IMDS is a composite index; 36 possible department pairs invite false alarms
:::

[A good brief reports the gap, its CI and its policy meaning, and says what the test cannot tell us.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter's Task 6 asks for a 200–300 word brief; its code cell builds the department summary table shown on the Task 3 slide. Tarija's CI is 7.4 points wide and Pando's 7.1. Key Concepts 4.12 and 4.13 both apply.
:::

# Reading it right {#synth .divider background-color="#C21E72"}

[Act III · The resolution]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Synthesis: put every test on one ruler, revisit the thread (real? matters? could we tell?), choose the right test, and leave with a checklist.
:::

## Every test in the deck on one ruler

![Test statistics from sections 4.4–4.7 and both case studies. Inside the shaded band, $\lvert t \rvert < 1.96$: no rejection at 5%.](figures/fig_tests_ruler.png)

[The same ±1.96 band decides every verdict. What changes is what the gap means.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
All numbers are from the slides above. Note the two bars for Case Study 1, Task 2: the same mean change gives t = 4.69 when the two years are wrongly treated as independent samples and t = 10.90 when they are correctly paired.
:::

## The thread, case by case: real? matters? could we tell? {.smaller}

| Test | Real? | Matters? | Could we tell? |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Gas vs \$3.81 | yes, $t = -5.26$ | yes, ≈ \$109/year | yes: tiny SE |
| Female earnings vs \$40k | no, $t = 0.72$ | possibly | **no**: power 0.11 at \$41,413 |
| Male earnings vs \$50k | no, $t = 0.50$ | possibly | **no**: SE \$4,706 from heavy tails |
| GDP growth vs 2% | no, $t = -0.07$ | yes, 1 pp compounds | **less than it looks**: autocorrelation 0.87 |
| Poll vs 50% | no, $z = 1.29$ | yes, elections are close | not at $n = 921$; just at 2,500 |
| CS1 2014 vs 1990 | yes, paired $t = 10.9$ | yes, +\$17,753 | yes, once paired |
| CS2 IMDS vs 50 | yes, $t = 3.13$ | [barely: 1.2 points]{.key} | yes: $n = 333$ |
| CS2 Tarija vs Pando | yes, $t = 6.29$ | yes, 14.7 points | yes, despite $n$ = 11, 13 |

[Significance answers only the first column. A complete answer fills in all three.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The recurring thread of the deck in one table. Note the two "no" rows in the third column: when we cannot tell, a non-rejection is uninformative, and the confidence interval is the honest summary.
:::

## Choosing the right test {.smaller}

| Situation | Test | Python | Example |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| One mean vs a value | one-sample $t$ | `stats.ttest_1samp` | earnings vs \$40,000 |
| Directional claim, fixed in advance | one-sided $t$ | `alternative="greater"` | La Paz vs national mean |
| Two independent groups | Welch two-sample $t$ | `stats.ttest_ind(…, equal_var=False)` | Africa vs Europe |
| Same units measured twice | paired $t$ | `stats.ttest_rel` | 1990 vs 2014, same countries |
| Yes/no outcome | proportion $z$ | `stats.norm` | voters, growth winners |
| Many comparisons | adjust $\alpha$ | Bonferroni $\alpha/k$ | 10 regional pairs |
| Dependent over time | HAC SEs (Ch. 12, 17) | — | GDP growth |

[Match the test to how the data were generated: independence, pairing, direction and the number of tests all matter.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Welch's version is a safe default for two groups; the pooled version assumes equal variances. The last row is a pointer: the chapter's GDP test assumes independence that the data do not have.
:::

## The tempting mistakes — and the corrections

[Objection.]{.objection} "$p < 0.05$, so the effect is real and important; $p > 0.05$, so there is no effect."

. . .

[Response.]{.rebuttal} Bolivia's mean IMDS differs "significantly" from 50 by 1.2 points: real but unimportant. Female earnings were not significantly above \$40,000, yet the test had an 11% chance of detecting a \$1,400 gap: no rejection, but no evidence of no effect either.

[Report the estimate and its confidence interval first; the $p$-value is a footnote to them.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter's "Common Mistakes to Avoid": a p-value is not the probability that H0 is true; statistical significance is not practical importance; a one-sided test needs prior justification.
:::

## Five questions to ask of any test

::: {.incremental}
1. **What exactly is $H_0$**, and is the claim of interest in $H_a$? Was the direction fixed in advance?
2. **Are the observations independent?** Repeated units call for pairing; time series and clusters need other SEs
3. **How big is the gap**, in units that matter (dollars, points, percentage points)?
4. **How wide is the CI**, and what is the power? Could the test have detected a gap that matters?
5. **How many tests were run?** Ten tests at 5% raise the chance of a false alarm to about 40%
:::

[These five questions turn a $p$-value from a verdict into evidence.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
A checklist students can apply to every inference table in the rest of the book. Questions 2 and 4 are the ones the chapter's own GDP and earnings examples needed most.
:::

## What to carry forward

::: {.incremental}
- The **standard error** $s/\sqrt{n}$ drives every interval and test, and it shrinks only with $\sqrt{n}$
- Use the **$t$ distribution** when $\sigma$ is estimated; by $n \approx 100$ it is close to the normal
- A **95% CI** is the set of values a two-sided 5% test would not reject; read it as a repeated-sampling statement
- $t = (\text{estimate} - \text{hypothesized value})/\text{SE}$: the recipe for every test in Chapters 7–17
- **Fail to reject ≠ accept**: check power and the CI before concluding "no effect"
- **Real, matters, could we tell?** Ask all three of every result
:::

::: {.notes}
Recap of the chapter's Key Takeaways, updated with what the deck verified: power, pairing, multiple testing and dependence.
:::
